title: Body Language and the Search for Hidden Meaning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post takes aim at the popular belief that gestures such as folded arms or a scratched nose reliably reveal what people are thinking. After acknowledging that nonverbal expression carries much of a message's feel, it flatly states there is no credible study behind gesture-decoding claims. Meaning is context dependent, and even lying shows up better as a deviation from a person's normal behavior than as any single tell. We use body language to confirm what we already believe, which the author labels confirmation bias. The practical lesson for leaders reading people is to distrust single-gesture interpretations and the media experts who sell them.
points: No credible research supports reading specific mental states from individual gestures.
Body language accentuates messages rather than carrying them, and no gesture means anything apart from context.
Watching for deviations from a person's normal behavior is more reliable than looking for universal tells.
Interpreting gestures often just feeds confirmation bias about what we already think.
quotes: Experts tell us that roughly 80 percent of the meaning of a message lies in the nonverbal expression of it.
Unless your local palm reader convinces you otherwise, it is time to discard this claim. There is not a shred of science that supports it. Not one credible study.
Even lying is associated with so many varied gestures it is more reliable to watch for deviations from what a person does normally than to look for the Pinocchio nose giveaway.
People use body language to accentuate messages, not to carry them. No one gesture or physical expression means anything void of the context within which it is created.
We use body language to confirm what we are already learning from others.
We simply can’t decode the mental states of others exclusively from their body language.
